personas.role: Fixed pole. Always argues from rights, always for the full market policy.
Swing, market side. Practical card is silent on the standard; common-good card names it.
Swing, control side. Practical card: experts should manage it. Moral card: borrows rights vocabulary for a collective conclusion.
Fixed pole. Always argues morally, always for control. Also the opposition slot every crisis.

crises.title: Drought
crises.trigger: The whole valley is in a drought. All the farms pump from the same water under the ground, and there isn't enough for everyone. While the drought lasts, your thirsty crops (the ones that need lots of water) grow only half as much.

policies.name: Farms can buy and sell water
policies.immediate: You can buy and sell water. In a drought, buying water costs 12 coins for each thirsty crop, and selling your water earns 6 coins for each one.
policies.drag: None

policies.name: Every farm can build its own well
policies.immediate: You can build your own well. In a drought, it waters your thirsty crops. But every farm pumps hard, and that drains the water under the valley. So the next drought lasts two seasons.
policies.drag: None

policies.name: A public water company does the pumping
policies.immediate: A public water company now pumps water for the whole valley. So any well on your farm is sealed. While this drought lasts, the company sells you water for just what it costs to pump.
policies.drag: From now on, you pay a water bill. Any well on your farm stays sealed. You can't build a new well, and you can't buy or sell water.
policies.modifier: waterAtCost: this drought; feePerTick: small; sealedBuildings: [well]; lockedActions: [drillWell, tradeWater]

policies.name: A water board with a rising water tax
policies.immediate: The water board now does all the pumping. So any well on your farm is sealed. You pay a tax on every gallon the board pumps for you, and the tax goes up as you use more. Only about 60% of your thirsty crops get water. The rest dry up and die.
policies.drag: The rising water tax stays. From now on, only about 60% of your thirsty crops get water each season, and the rest die. Any well on your farm stays sealed. You can't build a new well, and you can't buy or sell water.
policies.modifier: waterTax: rises per unit pumped; effective irrigationCap ≈ 0.6 × planted; sealedBuildings: [well]; lockedActions: [tradeWater, drillWell]

policies.name: Water handed out by need
policies.immediate: Water is handed out by need. Your farm gets water for only about 40% of your thirsty crops. The rest die. Your well is sealed.
policies.drag: Your water stays limited to about 40% of your thirsty crops. Your well stays sealed. You can't buy or sell water.

crises.title: Crop disease
crises.trigger: A crop disease is spreading through the valley. It came from bad seed, and every farm that plants that seed spreads the disease to the farms next door. It already killed one of your crops, and you can't plant that crop again for two planting seasons.

policies.name: Buy any seed, safe or not
policies.immediate: You can now buy premium seed. It costs 50% more, and you harvest 30% more from it. But about one planting in eight has the disease and dies.
policies.drag: None

policies.name: Sellers may add a 'checked safe' label
policies.immediate: Seed sellers hurry to get the 'checked safe' label. Buyers pay more for seed with the label. So soon almost all seed has the label, and it costs more.
policies.drag: From now on, seed costs about a quarter more.

policies.name: You pay the county to check seed
policies.immediate: The county now checks your seed, so it's safe to replant sooner. You can plant your lost crop again after one planting season, not two.
policies.drag: You pay a fee every time you plant. Checked seed costs about a quarter more. It is treated to stop the disease, so you harvest 10% less. To keep the disease out of the soil, you can't plant the same crop twice in a row on one plot. If you break that rule, you pay a fine.

policies.name: You need a permit and checked seed
policies.immediate: Every farm's seed is checked, so the disease can't come back to your fields. You can plant your lost crop again right away.
policies.drag: You pay a fee every time you plant. Checked seed costs about a quarter more. It is treated to stop the disease, so you harvest 10% less. You need a permit to plant. Get it at the council office the season before you plant. You can't plant the same crop twice in a row on one plot. If you plant without a permit, or plant the same crop twice in a row, you pay a fine.
policies.modifier: recoverySeasons: 0; feePerPlanting; permitDelayTicks on plant; cropRotation; seedCostMult: 1.25; yieldMult: 0.9

policies.name: A valley seed board picks your crops
policies.immediate: All your seed is now free. Each season, the seed board chooses one crop for you to grow.
policies.drag: The seed board decides what you grow. You harvest 20% less from every crop. If you plant any other crop, you pay a fine.

crises.title: Prices drop
crises.trigger: People across the country have less money to spend, so buyers pay less for crops. For the next two seasons, you get 40% less for everything you sell. Some farmers in the valley will lose their farms.

policies.name: Leave prices alone
policies.immediate: None
policies.drag: None

policies.name: Let farmers agree on next year's price with buyers
policies.immediate: While prices are low, you can make a deal with buyers to get 85% of the normal price for the next four seasons. If prices go back up before the four seasons end, you still get only 85%.
policies.drag: None

policies.name: Loans that farmers pay back later
policies.immediate: You get a loan now.
policies.drag: You pay it back over the next four seasons.

policies.name: A harvest tax pays to hold prices up
policies.immediate: Your prices drop only 10%, not 40%. The valley relief fund pays for the difference.
policies.drag: From now on, 10% of the coins from every harvest go into the valley relief fund.

policies.name: The government buys all crops at set prices
policies.immediate: Prices stay where they were before the drop.
policies.drag: You can sell only to the government, at a price that never goes up. Each season the government allows only a set number of sales, and that number changes every season. Sales over it earn no coins and don't count toward upgrades. Seed costs 50% more.

crises.title: Land for a dam
crises.trigger: The county is building a dam on the river to make a new lake. The lake will give the towns down the river water all year. The plan runs right through your east fields.

policies.name: The county builds only on its own land
policies.immediate: None
policies.drag: None

policies.name: Buy only if the owner says yes
policies.immediate: The county offers to buy 4 plots at the edge of your farm. It will pay 20% more than they're worth. You can say no.
policies.drag: None

policies.name: Take the land, pay full price
policies.immediate: The county takes 4 plots at the edge of your farm. It pays you full price. You can't say no.
policies.drag: None

policies.name: Take the land, pay half price
policies.immediate: The county takes 6 plots from all over your farm. It pays you half of what they're worth. Water from your fields runs into the new lake. To keep the lake clean, the county now has to approve what you build. It also decides what you plant. From now on, all seed is free.
policies.drag: The county has to approve new buildings and upgrades. So they take one season longer to build. You need a permit to plant. Get it at the council office the season before you plant. Each season the county picks the one crop you may plant. All seed is free. You pay a fine if you plant anything else or plant without a permit.
policies.modifier: removeTiles: {count: 6, selection: random, cashPerTile: 0.5×}; permitDelayTicks on plant; cropChoiceLocked: true; freeSeed: true

policies.name: Take the best land, pay nothing
policies.immediate: The county picks the land it wants. It takes your 8 best plots and pays you nothing. Water from the rest of your land runs into the new lake. So the county now decides what you plant on your land. From now on, all seed is free.
policies.drag: The county limits building on your farm. You can't build more of any kind of building than you have now, or any kind you don't have yet. Trees don't count. You need a permit to plant. Get it at the council office the season before you plant. Each season the county picks the one crop you may plant. All seed is free. You pay a fine if you plant anything else or plant without a permit.
policies.modifier: removeTiles: {count: 8, selection: mostProductive, cashPerTile: 0}; permitDelayTicks on plant; cropChoiceLocked: true; freeSeed: true

crises.note: Survey stakes appear; no farm effect until a policy passes.

crises.title: Too much of one crop
crises.trigger: Your farm had its best year ever. Now there's so much of your top crop for sale that its price has already dropped 25%. Other farmers say they can't sell their own crops because of you. They want the council to do something.

policies.name: No new rules
policies.immediate: None
policies.drag: None

policies.name: Farmers can choose to grow less together
policies.immediate: A group of farmers offers you a deal. If every member grows less of the top crop, the price goes back up. Then you'd get 15% more for yours. In return, you must grow it on 5 plots or fewer. You can say no.
policies.drag: You can grow your top crop on 5 plots at most. That's your part of the deal.

policies.name: A fee for each top-crop plot over 5
policies.immediate: You pay a fee for every plot of your top crop after the first 5. While more than 5 plots of it are planted, you have to wait a season to sell it.
policies.drag: You keep paying the fee for every plot of your top crop after the first 5. While more than 5 plots of it are planted, you must wait a season to sell it.

policies.name: The farm office limits planting and sales
policies.immediate: Your top crop is destroyed on every plot after the first 5. The county farm office now limits how much each farm sells, so every farm gets its turn. When the price drop ends, the office locks every crop at the normal price it has today.
policies.drag: You can't grow your top crop on more than 5 plots. One plot in five must stay empty each season. Breaking either rule costs a fine. Each season you can make about one sale for every two plots you have. Sales over that number earn nothing and don't count toward upgrades. Crop prices never go up, even when you improve your farm.
policies.modifier: destroyCrop: {crop: top, aboveTiles: 5}; maxTilesPerCrop: {top: 5}; fallow: 0.2; quota (steady); priceFixed: current

policies.name: Ban the crop and take what's above average
policies.immediate: Your top crop is banned. Every plot of it is destroyed.
policies.drag: At every harvest, you earn no more for a crop than the average farm in the valley does. Anything above that is taken. Crop prices never go up. Your buildings can't be upgraded. Each season the council sets a limit on how many sales you can make, and the limit changes each season. Sales over the limit earn nothing and don't count toward upgrades. Planting the banned crop costs a fine.
policies.modifier: destroyCrop: {crop: top, aboveTiles: 0}; banCrops: [top]; confiscateAboveAvg: 1.0; quota; priceFixed: current

crises.note: In the real game, trigger off farm value above a threshold.

cards.argument: You should own your part of the valley's water, just like you own your land. Then it's your choice to use it or sell it to a neighbor who wants to buy.
Let every farm build its own well and pump as much as it wants. That's the fastest way to save crops that need lots of water, because no farm has to wait for someone else to decide.
It's best for everyone if every farm can build its own well. Then small farms can save their crops too, not just the big ones.
The scientists know how much water we can pump without running out. Their plan is a water tax that rises as a farm uses more, so farms pump less and the water lasts.
Every farm, rich or poor, has a right to water at a price it can afford. So the first water each farm uses should be taxed only a little, and the tax should rise as it uses more.
This valley's water belongs to all of us, so we share it instead of selling it. Let's hand it out by what each farm needs and get through this drought together.
It's your farm, so you get to buy seed from any seller you like. If you pick risky seed and the crop dies, the loss is yours, because the choice was yours.
Farmers will pay more for seed with a 'checked safe' label. So sellers will want the label because it makes them more money, and safe seed will sell more than bad seed.
It's best for everyone if seed sellers can add a 'checked safe' label. Then every farm, big or small, can tell which seed is safe and buy what it can pay for.
The county's seed experts can find the disease before it spreads. Their tests show that the fastest way to stop it is to check every farm's seed and make farms get a permit to plant.
Every family in the valley, rich or poor, has a right to a safe harvest. So every farm is owed a seed test, and no farm may plant until its seed passes and the farm has a permit.
The food we grow belongs to all of us, so we should protect it together. One valley seed board should give every farm the same free seed and choose what each farm plants.
Your crop belongs to you, so you can sell it at any price you and a buyer both choose. If the council leaves prices alone, you decide whether to sell now, wait, or grow something else.
Prices are down 40%, and no one knows for how long. If farmers can agree on next year's price with buyers now, each farm knows what it will earn, so fewer farms run out of coins.
It is best for everyone if farmers can agree on next year's price with buyers now. Shoppers know what food will cost, and farmers know what they will earn.
Experts at the county farm office have a plan. A tax on every harvest should pay to hold prices at 90% of the old price, and their numbers show this saves the most farms.
Every farmer has a right to earn enough for food and a home, even when prices fall. So a tax on every harvest should pay for a valley fund that keeps crop prices from falling too far.
The food we grow belongs to all of us, so every farm should get the same fair deal. The government should buy every crop at the old price, from before the drop.
The county should put the dam and the lake on land it already owns. You own your fields, and nobody has the right to take them, even for a good reason.
The county should buy only from owners who want to sell, and pay a bit more than the land is worth. Owners who like that price say yes quickly, so work on the dam can start sooner.
The county should buy only from families who want to sell, because that's best for everyone. Families who sell get a good price, and families who stay keep farming.
The county's engineers measured the river, and their numbers show which land the lake needs and what to pay for it. The county should follow their plan, take that land and pay half price.
Every family down the river has a right to water all year, and the farmer is owed something for the land. So the county should take the land the lake needs and pay half price.
The land in this valley belongs to all of us, not just the family that farms it. So the county should take the best of it for the lake and pay nothing.
It's your land and your crop, and you chose to plant it. You're free to grow and sell as much as you want, so the council should make no new rules about it.
When there's too much of one crop, its price drops. If some farmers choose to team up and grow less of it, the price goes back up fast, and they could earn 15% more for their crop.
Farmers who join a group to grow less get a better price, and farmers who don't join keep growing plenty of food for families. That's best for everyone.
The county farm office keeps track of how much of each crop people buy. Its experts should use those numbers to set how much each farm plants and sells, so prices stay steady.
Every farm family is owed a fair chance to sell its crop. The county farm office should set a planting limit for each farm, so every farm can find buyers.
Ban this crop. And when any farm grows more food than the average farm, the extra belongs to all of us, and we share it equally.

answer.moral_rights: You stood up for your rights. You said the choice is yours to make. The council heard both sides, and you won that argument.
answer.practical: You showed your plan would work. But you never said why it was right. So the council heard only one argument about right and wrong. It was the one for more control.
answer.moral_common_good: You argued about what's best for everyone. The other side said more control is what's best for everyone. On that question, the council sided with more control.
answer.moral_positive_right: You argued for more control yourself.
answer.moral_collective: You argued for more control yourself.
